questions.question_text:
A particle has acceleration $\underset{\sim}{a}(t)=10t\,\underset{\sim}{i}-6\underset{\sim}{j}$ and $\underset{\sim}{v}(0)=-4\underset{\sim}{i}+2\underset{\sim}{j}$.
Which vector is $\underset{\sim}{v}(t)$?

options.why: Left the constant of integration out of the i component; the constant is a vector, so every component needs one.
Left the constant of integration out of the j component; the constant is a vector, so every component needs one.
Took the constant of integration to be zero and ignored the given initial velocity entirely.

questions.question_text:
A particle has acceleration $\underset{\sim}{a}(t)=4\underset{\sim}{i}+6t\,\underset{\sim}{j}$, with $\underset{\sim}{v}(0)=2\underset{\sim}{i}-\underset{\sim}{j}$ and $\underset{\sim}{r}(0)=\underset{\sim}{i}+3\underset{\sim}{j}$.
Which vector is $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)$?

options.why: Omitted the i component of the second (position) constant of integration.
Omitted the j component of the second (position) constant of integration.
Used the initial velocity but then assumed $\underset{\sim}{r}(0)=\underset{\sim}{0}$ instead of the given initial position.

questions.question_text:
A particle has acceleration $\underset{\sim}{a}(t)=6\underset{\sim}{i}-4\underset{\sim}{j}$, with $\underset{\sim}{v}(0)=-2\underset{\sim}{i}+5\underset{\sim}{j}$ and $\underset{\sim}{r}(0)=\underset{\sim}{0}$.
What is $\underset{\sim}{r}(2)$?

options.why: Substituted $t=2$ into the j component of the velocity instead of the position.
Substituted $t=2$ into the i component of the velocity instead of the position.
Stopped after the first integration and gave $\underset{\sim}{v}(2)$ rather than $\underset{\sim}{r}(2)$.

questions.question_text:
A particle has acceleration $\underset{\sim}{a}(t)=8t\,\underset{\sim}{i}+2\underset{\sim}{j}$ and $\underset{\sim}{v}(1)=6\underset{\sim}{i}+5\underset{\sim}{j}$.
Which vector is $\underset{\sim}{v}(t)$?

options.why: Read the i component of the condition as if it were given at $t=0$, so $c_{1}=6$ instead of $2$.
Read the j component of the condition as if it were given at $t=0$, so $c_{2}=5$ instead of $3$.
Treated the condition as $\underset{\sim}{v}(0)=6\underset{\sim}{i}+5\underset{\sim}{j}$ and read both constants straight off.

questions.question_text:
A particle has acceleration $\underset{\sim}{a}(t)=-8\sin 2t\,\underset{\sim}{i}+12\cos 2t\,\underset{\sim}{j}$ and $\underset{\sim}{v}(0)=4\underset{\sim}{i}$.
Which vector is $\underset{\sim}{v}(t)$?

options.why: Multiplied by $2$ instead of dividing by $2$ when integrating the i component.
Multiplied by $2$ instead of dividing by $2$ when integrating the j component.
Multiplied each component by $2$ rather than dividing by $2$ when reversing the chain rule.

questions.question_text:
A particle has acceleration $\underset{\sim}{a}(t)=12t^{2}\underset{\sim}{i}+2\underset{\sim}{j}$, with $\underset{\sim}{v}(0)=\underset{\sim}{0}$ and $\underset{\sim}{r}(0)=-\underset{\sim}{i}+4\underset{\sim}{j}$.
Which vector is $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)$?

options.why: Took the i component of $\underset{\sim}{r}(0)$ as $+1$ rather than $-1$.
Integrated $2t$ as $2t^{2}$ instead of $t^{2}$.
Integrated $2t$ as $2t^{2}$ and also read the initial position as $\underset{\sim}{i}+4\underset{\sim}{j}$.

questions.question_text:
A particle has acceleration $\underset{\sim}{a}(t)=-6\underset{\sim}{i}+12t\,\underset{\sim}{j}$ and position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(7t-3t^{2})\underset{\sim}{i}+(2t^{3}-5t+4)\underset{\sim}{j}$.
What is the initial velocity of the particle?

options.why: Read the j component from $\underset{\sim}{r}(0)$ instead of differentiating to get $\dot{y}(0)=-5$.
Read the i component from $\underset{\sim}{r}(0)$ instead of differentiating to get $\dot{x}(0)=7$.
Gave the initial position $\underset{\sim}{r}(0)$ rather than the initial velocity.

questions.question_text:
A particle moves with acceleration $\underset{\sim}{a}(t)=-10\underset{\sim}{j}$ for $t\ge 0$.
It starts at the origin with velocity $12\underset{\sim}{i}+25\underset{\sim}{j}$.
What is its position vector at the instant when it is moving parallel to $\underset{\sim}{i}$?

options.why: Found $t=2.5$ correctly but integrated $25-10t$ as $25t$, dropping the $-5t^{2}$ term.
Solved $25t-5t^{2}=0$, the time it returns to the starting level, instead of $25-10t=0$.
Solved $25t-5t^{2}=0$ to get $t=5$ and then evaluated the j component as $25t$, dropping the $-5t^{2}$ term.

questions.solution_text:
$\underset{\sim}{v}(t)$
$=12\underset{\sim}{i}+(25-10t)\underset{\sim}{j}$
Moving parallel to $\underset{\sim}{i}$ means the j component of the velocity is zero.
$25-10t=0$
$t=2.5$
$\underset{\sim}{r}(t)$
$=12t\,\underset{\sim}{i}+(25t-5t^{2})\underset{\sim}{j}$
$\underset{\sim}{r}(2.5)$
$=30\underset{\sim}{i}+(62.5-31.25)\underset{\sim}{j}$
$=30\underset{\sim}{i}+31.25\underset{\sim}{j}$
